headline: Kryzz AI app sends first message to different model for chat titles, developer reveals privacy detail
summary: Kryzz AI, an Android chat app, sends the initial part of your first message to Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite via OpenRouter to generate chat titles, a detail the developer transparently disclosed. This occurs even if you've selected a different primary provider.
details: Kryzz AI, an MIT-licensed Android app, offers chat, voice, and agent tasks with a strong focus on on-device privacy. It keeps chats, memory, files, and API keys encrypted locally, with no analytics or telemetry. Users bring their own OpenRouter key for model access.

Despite its privacy-first design, the developer revealed a specific detail about chat title generation. When a new chat starts, the app automatically names it by sending the first 1,500 characters of the initial message to a model.
This title generation uses Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite through the user's OpenRouter key, running in parallel with the main chat response. If this process fails, the app falls back to a local title.

The developer emphasized that while it uses the same key and route, it's a second request to a potentially different model than the user's primary choice. This disclosure was made to ensure complete transparency, as "no telemetry" is only meaningful if all data flows are accounted for.
The app is currently not on the Play Store or F-Droid, requiring users to build from source. The latest signed release has only been tested on an Android 15 emulator, with bug reports welcomed.

headline_marked: [[Claude AI surprisingly speeds up old Google TV]] by debloating with minimal user input
headline: Claude AI surprisingly speeds up old Google TV by debloating with minimal user input
summary: An Android Police editor used Claude Code to automatically debloat and optimize their slow Google TV devices, freeing up storage and RAM with surprising ease and minimal effort.
details: Android TVs and low-end streaming boxes often slow down significantly over time, becoming frustratingly sluggish. This common issue led an editor to try a viral method involving Claude AI to revitalize old devices.

Previously, the idea of debloating Android TVs seemed too convoluted and time-consuming, despite knowing it could improve performance. However, seeing others successfully use Claude on X prompted a personal experiment.

The process began with a Mi Box S running Android 9, which had become painfully slow with only about 1GB of free space. The goal was to see if Claude could simplify the complex task of removing unnecessary software.

After enabling ADB on the Mi Box S, a Claude Code instance was launched on a Mac. A simple prompt, "Find the Mi Box streaming box on my network. I have ADB enabled. Check if you can access it," initiated the process.

Claude intelligently detected the missing ADB installation on the Mac and proceeded to install it via Homebrew. It then scanned the home network, located the Mi Box, and established a connection after the user approved the USB debugging prompt on the TV.

With access granted, Claude scanned the installed software, identified non-critical system packages, and generated a list of bloatware for removal. Crucially, it recommended a reversible method, leaving essential OS and Google framework packages untouched.

The AI even listed preinstalled streaming apps and asked the user to select which ones to uninstall. In one instance, Claude suggested removing Xiaomi's PatchWall launcher for a significant speed boost, a trade-off the user accepted for a faster experience.

Within minutes, Claude successfully debloated the Mi Box S, removing unnecessary packages and freeing up storage and RAM. It also offered further optimizations like disabling background cache and animations, though these were declined.

The entire process felt remarkably smooth and required minimal user input, making a previously daunting task straightforward. The editor replicated the success on other old Android and Google TVs in their home.

Claude's ability to handle the technical setup and cleanup, while still allowing the user to decide what to keep or remove, bridged the gap of complexity. This convenience finally enabled the editor to tackle a long-deferred optimization project.
